title: Working with metallic and specialty thread
subtitle: How to handle metallic, silk, and overdyed thread without tangles and snapping.
excerpt: Metallic thread snaps, tangles, and frays more readily than stranded cotton. Shorter lengths, a larger needle, and a slower rhythm solve most of the problems.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Specialty thread notes and handling.
Weldon's Practical Needlework, volume 3 (1888), Internet Archive. Gold and metal thread work notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: Embroidery thread with a metal-coated outer ply or a metallic core. More brittle than cotton thread; requires a shorter working length and a larger needle to reduce friction.
Embroidery thread dyed with multiple colours in sequence along the skein, producing subtle colour shifts across the worked stitches without the stitcher changing thread.

content.text: Metallic thread is brittle and has more friction against the cloth than cotton. The main adjustment is cutting shorter lengths, about 25 to 30 cm, and slowing the pull-through on each stitch. A
pulled quickly through many layers of cloth frays and breaks at the needle eye before the end of a single thread length.

items.name: Embroidery needle, size 7 (one size larger than normal)
Metallic or specialty thread, cut to 25 to 30 cm lengths

content.text: Cut lengths of 25 to 30 cm. Longer lengths snap from friction before reaching the end.
Use a needle one size larger than you would normally use for the cloth count. The larger eye reduces friction at the thread's most-worked point.
Thread the needle with the thread tail no longer than 8 cm. A long tail tangles behind the needle.
Pull each stitch through slowly and gently. Metallic thread does not like being dragged quickly through the cloth.
Store metallic thread in a cool, dry place in its original tube or bobbin. Flat storage prevents the twist from loosening.

behaves exactly like standard stranded cotton but is much more sensitive to where stitching starts along the skein. Two threads cut from different points in the colour repeat can look completely different in the finished piece. Cut all the lengths for a section from the same part of the skein before beginning, or accept the variation as part of the look.

attrs.heading: What goes wrong
attrs.intro: Problems specific to metallic and specialty threads.

items.symptom: The thread snaps near the needle eye
items.cause: The thread is too long (25+ passes through the cloth have stressed the section near the eye), or the needle is too small.
items.fix: Shorten the working length to 25 cm and move up one needle size.

items.symptom: The thread twists and kinks badly
items.cause: The needle is rotating as it is pulled through, adding twist.
items.fix: After every four or five stitches, let the needle hang free to untwist. Metallic threads need this much more often than cotton.

items.symptom: The metallic outer layer strips away from the core
items.cause: The scissors used to cut the thread have nicks or are too blunt.
items.fix: Use embroidery scissors kept exclusively for thread work. A blunt blade crushes rather than cuts, stripping the metallic coating.

content.text: Metallic thread skills apply to goldwork, cross-stitch borders, and mixed-thread surface embroidery. This guide also covers blending filaments such as Kreinik used alongside stranded cotton.
